key_insight: Correcting dataset bias in binding-affinity data substantially improves out-of-distribution generalization of prediction models; bias-aware data curation and evaluation reveal true model performance rather than spurious correlations.
problem_solved: Public binding-affinity benchmarks contain selection and distributional biases (uneven target/ligand representation, correlated experimental conditions) that cause models to overfit and produce overly optimistic results on standard test splits, reducing real-world utility.
method: Diagnose and quantify dataset biases (e.g., target/ligand frequency imbalances and confounding experimental variables).
Apply bias-resolution procedures: curated filtering, reweighting or stratified splitting to remove spurious correlations and produce more realistic training/test partitions.
Re-evaluate models on bias-aware, out-of-distribution (OOD) splits and corrected baselines to demonstrate improved generalization.
impact: Adopting bias-aware curation and evaluation yields more reliable binding-affinity predictors for drug discovery and reduces false confidence from biased benchmarks; it promotes reproducible, transferable ML models in molecular sciences.
visual_elements: Heatmap showing dataset composition by target and ligand frequency to illustrate imbalance.
Before/after bar chart comparing OOD performance (e.g., RMSE or Spearman) with original vs bias-corrected data.
Pipeline diagram of bias-identification → curation/reweighting → OOD evaluation.
Scatter plots of predicted vs true affinities showing tighter correlation after bias correction.
paper_title: Addendum: Resolving data bias improves generalization in binding affinity prediction
paper_authors: David Graber, Peter Stockinger, Fabian Meyer, Siddhartha Mishra, Claus Horn
